2313.prule: Penultimate. Every polysyllabic phonological word (micro-segment, 1-6 syllables) is accented (stress + raised pitch) on its penultimate syllable; monosyllabic free morphemes are accented, bound monosyllables are not. quantity-insensitive: vowel length is stated to function independently of stress. Robinson 1970 p. 1: 'Placement of primary stress is on the penultimate syllable of the word - except for a few patterns of ultimate and antepenultimate placement.'
2313.srule: Placed by morphology, not rhythmic (Robinson 1969): in a compounded or suffixed word the main accent is on the penult of the final micro-segment and each non-final constituent (every root of a compound; the base of a suffixed form) keeps its own penult accent reduced to 'tertiary accent': 'pico-"nákat 'pork', 'to"kámeh 'spiders', ki'či"wáti 'he goes to do it', šaša'wa"káya 'it was rustling', 'kita"tóya 'he was seeing it'. A simple word (stem ± the post-clitics -ti/-sah/-ok/-ya) has one accent; its 1-4 pretonic and 1-3 post-tonic syllables are 'unstressed' (MiS formulas), so there is no rhythmic secondary stress at any length.

2318.prule: Primary stress (marked ˈ, carrying the metrical high tone) falls on the second syllable of the underlying word in words of three or more underlying syllables (= moras), and on the first syllable of morphologically simple disyllabic (bimoraic) words. The source counts moras, but in its own analysis the mora equals the vowel (p. 237), every vowel is its own syllable nucleus ((C)V(N) underlyingly, p. 175; (C)(R)V(C)(T) on the surface, p. 182; no VV-nucleus type in Tables 4.1-4.2), vowel sequences are syllabified heterosyllabically (/paantama/ = pa.an.ta.ma, /maata/ = ma.a.ta, /pɨaka/ = pɨ.a.ka, /maaitahai/ = ma.a.i.ta.ha.i) and codas are 'irrelevant for stress and tone assignment'. So 'the second mora receives the metrical high tone' = second underlying syllable, quantity-insensitive: left-to-right disyllabic iambs (W S), head of the leftmost foot stressed: (na.ˈma).ka -> [namák] 'fish', (pa.ˈan)(ta.ma) -> [paántam] 'plantain', (maˈa).ta -> [maát] 'to bathe', (pɨ.ˈa).ka -> [pɨák] 'bed', (ku.ˈhan)(t͡ʃa.ma) -> [kuhánt͡ʃam], (t͡ʃi.ˈt͡ʃa)(sa.ta)(sa.nu) -> [t͡ʃit͡ʃástasan]; simple bimoraic words take the high tone on the first mora by last-mora extrametricality ([ápa] 'father', [númi] 'tree', [húka] 'PROX=FOC'). Feet are formed at an intermediate stage after glide formation and morpheme-boundary sandhi but before vowel elision; pervasive elision of weak-position vowels makes surface stress frequently word-final or on a closed syllable ([namák], [kuhánt͡ʃam], [t͡sawán]), so the grid is over underlying vowels/syllables, not surface syllables.
2318.srule: Notation only: Peña 2015 parses words exhaustively into left-to-right iambs and writes ˌ on the head of every non-initial foot (4th, 6th... underlying mora; schematic (CV.ˈCV)(CV.ˌC.V)(CV.ˌCV)CV... p. 244, 'for the most part applicable synchronically'; (aˈru)(taˌma) -> [arútam] p. 253; (taˈka)(saˌta)(haˌi) -> [takástahɛɛ] p. 256), but he describes no phonetic secondary stress: only ˈ 'primary stress' is defined (p. 244), 'secondary stress' is never mentioned, acoustic correlates are given for the tonic syllable only (6.4.3), no phonetic output carries ˌ, and the non-initial feet serve to predict vowel elision of weak positions (a ˌ-marked word-final vowel is itself apocopated in (17)).

The 'pitch-accent' label is explicitly rejected (sec. 6.7): 'Wampis is not a prototypical stress language nor is it a prototypical tone language, it has features of both ends of the continuum.'

2320.prule: Stress is phonemic, i.e. lexically contrastive by position (minimal pairs 'tuka 'day' / tu'ka 'spider', 'ʔaki 'rib' / ʔa'ki 'your house', pʌ'waki 'it is dry' / pʌwa'ki 'it is their house'); the last (main) stress of the word falls on the penult in the majority of words 'but by no means all of them'; when a morpheme that is not usually stressed occupies the penult, the final syllable is usually stressed instead.

2322.tone: Mixtec varieties are tonal; Carroll p. 86 describes the couplet as 'a unit of two tonemes' in Pike's San Miguel el Grande analysis and as bimoraic where monomoraic tone contours are permitted. Huitepec-specific tone is reported only indirectly in this entry's source list (Josserand's tone-marked wordlists per MixteCoDB; Julián Caballero 2009:266 'un leve cambio de tono' for tense). No source denies stress for Huitepec, and the carried family statement asserts stress alongside tone, so not tone or pitch accent.

tn.quote: Otros ejemplos sobre la complejidad del tu’un savi es en cuanto a los verbos de movimiento: Del verbo subir en tu’un savi hay que tomar en cuenta los tonos y los tiempos verbales: “ñee” que significa “subió” (tiempo pasado) y “sube” (tiempo presente) con un leve cambio de tono y para superar este problema con quienes no conocen la lengua se recurren los adverbios de tiempo (iku=ayer, kani=antier, ndekani=antes de antier, vitna=hoy, en este momento, navii=ahorita) y para el tiempo futuro es “kaa” ...
tn.translation: Other examples of the complexity of Tu'un Savi concern the verbs of motion: for the verb 'to go up' in Tu'un Savi one has to take into account the tones and the verb tenses: 'ñee', which means 'went up' (past tense) and 'goes up' (present tense) with a slight change of tone, and to get over this problem with those who do not know the language one resorts to the time adverbs (iku = yesterday, kani = the day before yesterday, ndekani = before that, vitna = today, at this moment, navii = right now), and for the future tense it is 'kaa' ...

2325.heavy: Four-level hierarchy CVV > CVC > CV > CVH: long vocoids (long vowels and vowel+glide) heaviest and stress-attracting anywhere in the word; CVC = short vowel plus a coda other than /h/ or glottal stop, heavier than CV only within the root in the modern data (prefixal CVC does not attract stress); syllables closed by /h/ or glottal stop (CVH) lightest, optionally rejecting stress.
2325.dflt: Modern data: the root syllable (necessarily CVV or CVC; in polysyllabic roots the leftmost CVC, CVH roots optionally yielding to the initial syllable). Sapir data: the initial syllable when the first two syllables are of equal weight.
2325.prule: Modern Hupa (1995 isolated words): primary stress on the leftmost long vocoid (CVV, incl. vowel+glide) anywhere in the word; if the word has no long vowel, stress on the root syllable (monosyllabic roots are obligatorily CVV/CVC); within a polysyllabic root the leftmost CVC (coda other than /h/, glottal stop) over CV; root syllables closed by /h/ or glottal stop optionally pass stress to the word-initial syllable. Weight scale CVV > CVC > CV > CVH. Sapir's 1927 texts instead: stress on one of the first two syllables (91%), the heavier of the two by the same scale, initial syllable in ties, blind to root/affix status.
2325.srule: None found: the 1995 acoustic data 'failed to show convincing evidence for secondary stress' (non-primary long vowels are not consistently more intense or higher in f0 than unstressed short vowels); in Sapir's 1927 texts words with more than one stress mark are 'rare enough that no reliable inferences about the possibility of secondary stress are possible'.
2325.quote: [p.116] Both sets of data are sensitive to the same syllable weight hierarchy: CVV > CVC > CV > CVH. This weight hierarchy is manifested in different ways during the two stages of Hupa. In the more recent acoustic data, stress falls on the leftmost CVV syllable and on the root in the absence of any prefixal long vowels. Goddard 1928:338 (kymograph study): 'It does not seem that pitch or pitch change is used to differentiate between words similar in other respects... 2326.prule: Stem-initial stress of the German type: the first syllable of the word carries the stress 'almost absolutely' (Erstsilben-Betonung, as in German and English), so the dictionary leaves it unmarked; but when the first syllable is an inseparable (unstressable) prefix (ga-/ge-, fer-/ver-, also on hybrid English-based verbs like /gapelat/), the stress falls on the second syllable, i.e. the stem; any other placement (mainly in foreign words) is marked individually with an acute over the stressed vowel. Position is thus set by morphological structure (prefix vs. stem), not by syllable count or weight.

2327.heavy: Syllables whose nucleus is the low vowel /a/ ('usually of greater intensity', and per 2.1.3 'usually of longer duration than the other vowel phonemes') as against syllables with high /ɨ/ or mid /ə/.
2327.dflt: Not stated by Staalsen (nothing said about words containing only /ɨ/ and /ə/). Jendraschek 2012: 91-92: in disyllables of two short syllables 'there is a strong tendency to stress the first syllable'; for polysyllables 'Word-initial syllables are stressed' is ranked third among the general tendencies, after 'Long vowels are stressed' and 'CVC syllables are stressed'.
2327.prule: Staalsen 1966: 74 (Nyaura, Brugnowi): stress is non-phonemic and non-contrastive; where predictable at all it goes with the vowel, low /a/ (2.1.3: 'usually of longer duration than the other vowel phonemes') carrying greater intensity than /ɨ/ and /ə/; no positional rule, window or default stated; loudness peak and intonational pitch peak need not coincide. Jendraschek 2012: 91-93 (Korogo; read first-hand): word stress is 'a correlate of other factors like vowel length, syllable structure'; in disyllables a syllable with a long or half-long vowel (or /aʔ/) is stressed, otherwise 'a strong tendency to stress the first syllable', nearly neutralized when the second syllable is CVC; in polysyllables stress 'becomes unpredictable', with tendencies in decreasing importance: 1. long vowels stressed, 2. CVC syllables stressed, 3. word-initial syllables stressed, 4. in compounds the rules may apply to the second member ('Stress assignment to the first or second member is random'); diphthongs and phonetically long /e/ do not attract stress; wula'i and si'ba'i are stressed on the second syllable.
2327.srule: Not mentioned by Staalsen 1966 (sec. 5, pp. 74-75). Jendraschek 2012: when both members of a compound are polysyllabic the unstressed member is likely to carry secondary stress (avuktakwa [ˈaβukˌtaɰwɑ] 'old woman', abukava [ˈabuˌɡaβa] 'garden site'), and at slow-to-normal speech rate the same holds for non-compound words of four or more syllables (kwadamali [ˈkwandaˌmaɾi]); the number of intensity peaks depends on speech rate (several in slow speech, some reduced to 'secondary stress' at intermediate speed, a single peak in fast speech). 2329.prule: No word stress: Ibibio is a lexical-tone language that 'lacks stress prominence'. The only foot-like organisation is the verb stem's CVXCV template (first syllable heavy or light, second syllable light; full vowel contrasts only in the first syllable; lenition in the second), diagnosed by weight and segmental asymmetries, not by stress.
2329.srule: Not applicable: no word stress of any degree. Not mentioned in Harris, Urua & Tang 2023 (sections 4 and 6, pp. 43-47 and 58-59 read): 'As a lexical-tone language, Ibibio lacks stress prominence' (p. 43); likewise Akinlabi & Urua 2003: 'Ibibio does not have stress prominence' (p. 133).
2329.quote: In Ibibio, the basic template takes the form C1V1XC2V2, where X is a copy of either V1 (CVVCV) or C2 (CVCCV). The resemblance to a heavy-light trochee is unmistakable, as has been pointed out by Urua (1990, 2000) and Akinlabi & Urua (1992, 1994). Similar observations have been made about the closely related language Efik (Cook 1985; Hyman 1990). As a lexical-tone language, Ibibio lacks stress prominence, the property most usually associated with the metrical foot. Nevertheless, the CVXCV template does display weight and segmental asymmetries that are strongly reminiscent of trochees in stress…

2329.idn: Ibibio; the primary source names no dialect ('four adult native speakers of Ibibio'). The two companion works by co-author Urua name the Uruan variety: Urua 2004 'The variety presented here is spoken in Uruan area and Uyo'; Akinlabi & Urua 2003 'the Uruan dialect, as spoken in Mbaya, about eight miles from Uyo'.…
2329.exq_: It is debatable whether these facts indicate that Ibibio actually has metrical feet. The stem template might instead reflect a universally preferred prosodic shape for root+suffix combinations (Downing 2006).
2329.tone: Source calls Ibibio 'a lexical-tone language' and says it 'lacks stress prominence'; segmental asymmetries 'signal accentual prominence even in the absence of stress' (p. 58). Urua 2004 JIPA: 'Ibibio is a register terraced level tone language with two level tones (H)igh and (L)ow' with HL/LH contours and automatic/non-automatic downstep; the words stress/accent do not occur there. Gut, Urua, Adouakou & Gibbon 2002 (TAPS, p. 161): vowels undergo 'deletion but not reduction in the sense in which English vowels undergo reduction in unstressed syllables'. Gibbon 2022 (Festschrift Urua, p. 468) reads a low-frequency rhythm spectrum as 'indicating the presence of prosodic feet or stress groups in addition to syllable tone' -- an acoustic-rhythm inference, not a word-stress description.

tn.quote: Ibibio is a register terraced level tone language with two level tones (H)igh and (L)ow. Combinations of the level tones from tone spreading and segment deletion result in the formation of two types of contour tones, namely, High-Low and Low-High, which are not contrastive with each other. Ibibio also has a downstepped feature, which affects High tones, and manifests both automatic and non-automatic downstep. ... Tone performs both lexical and grammatical functions in the language.

2331.prule: No word-stress rule: Ife is a three-level register tone language (H, M, L); every syllable / every vowel and surface nasal is a tone-bearing unit; no downstep, no underlying contour tones. Stress or accent is not described in any reachable source.
2331.quote: [Kohler, Roberts, Harley & Sena 2025, sec. 1.4.3 'Tone', pp. 66-67] Like Yoruba, Ife has three discrete level tones (H, M, L) and all vowels as well as surface pre-consonantal and final nasals are tone bearing. 2331.idn: the Tchetti dialect of Ife (Togo), the principal dialect chosen for orthography standardization (Kohler et al. 2025: 62); Kohler 1983 and Boëthius 1983 likewise rest on the parler tchéti (speakers from Akparé, Anié, Atakpamé). Same language as the record (Ifè).
2331.tone: Three discrete level tones H, M, L (Kohler et al. 2025 p. 66; Kohler 1983 p. 141; Boëthius 1983 p. 112 'Chaque syllabe porte un ton haut, moyen ou bas'; Gblem-Poidi 2018 p. 13 'L'ifɛ est une langue tonale... trois hauteurs mélodiques'). Register (non-terracing) system: 'l'ifè est une langue à registres... n'a pas d'abaissement' (Kohler 1983: 139), confirmed 2025. Surface contour tones arise only from vowel/nasal elision and are prohibited on single moras. M tone elides next to H/L. Kohler 1983 describes tone schemes by word class and grammatical tone. The only 'force' remark (Kohler 1983 p. 151: 'la longueur ou la force du ton haut dépend du ton de la dernière syllabe du numéral') concerns the phonetic strength of the numeral-prefix H tone, not stress. No source mentions stress, accent or prominence.

X identifies a persistive qualifier prefix and Y encompasses contrasting perfective/ imperfective toneme suffixes. Tones from these suffixes spread onto lexically toneless verbs. 2332.tone: Tone language: lexical and grammatical H, L and downstepped H (p. 234); verbs are lexically toneless and take their tone from aspect suffixes (perfective -í with H; imperfective a floating L); orthography marks tone with acute, grave and acute+apostrophe (p. 262). The paper does not discuss stress (rather than denying it): a full-text search of the article for stress/accent/prominence finds only the diacritic sentence. The other held texts on the same language (Egbokhare 1989 JWAL 19.1 deictics; Donwa-Ifode 1990 JWAL 20.2 Ora phonology/orthography; Egbokhare 2002 ideophone chapter; Egbokhare 2011 inaugural lecture) contain no stress or accent statement either; Egbokhare 2011 mentions stress only for English and in a generic list of suprasegmentals, and says Emai tone has a high grammatical functional load.

The border point following the word is symbolized by space or hyphen (hyphen when the word is followed by one or more clitics.) ... The border point following a stress group is also a grammatical border point following a word-base and its affixes. In the intonation group, or phrase, the onset of the …
2334.prule: Stress is non-contrastive ('nonphonemic') and falls at the right edge of the stress group (word base plus affixes; post-clitics are stressed but lie outside it): on the penultimate or the final syllable, or, when a stressed suffix (-an, -ʌn, -i, -ʌy, -a) is present, on both final and penultimate or on both final and antepenultimate syllables (secs. 1.22-1.23, e.g. [ʔʌd'suli'tʌn] 'to correct (it)', ['duma'an] 'to accompany (him)'). Penultimate stress is the 'predominant pattern'; final stress is assigned segmentally: always when the penult vowel is followed by a homorganic semivowel (sec. 1.211), and, utterance-medially, in c. 40 listed templates defined by the vowels of the last two syllables and the consonant beginning (sometimes also closing) the final syllable (sec. 1.212), with free final~penult fluctuation utterance-finally or in isolation. Syllable weight plays no role; the position is not computable from syllable count alone.
2334.srule: No rhythmic or graded secondary stress is described (Shand never ranks stresses; unsuffixed, unreduplicated words carry one stress). A second stress within the stress group arises only with the stressed suffixes -an, -ʌn, -i, -ʌy, -a: final + penultimate stress when the suffix follows one of the sec. 1.212 sequences (or a semivowel, l, r, ŋ with the suffix group-final), e.g. [ʔi'kʌ'tan] 'rope', [bʌ'la'yan]; final + antepenultimate stress after any other sequence or when another syllable follows in the intonation group, e.g. ['duma'ʔan] 'to accompany (him)', ['bʌla'yan'daŋ]. Reduplicated bases repeat the base's stress ([mʌ'rayi'rayi] 'very good'); post-clitics bear their own stress outside the stress group.
